messages.content: Why is running `julia -e 'using MyPkg; check()'` after every edit so slow even when the package is already precompiled?

Compile cost is paid per process start, not per edit. Every `julia -e` launch starts a fresh runtime, loads the package, and compiles every specialization `check()` needs from scratch, even with a warm precompile cache (which only stores what the package's own precompile workload covered). Edit count does not matter; process count does.

Fix: keep one persistent process and send each check to it. With the JuliaMCP tools:

```text
1. julia_create_session  (project=/path/to/MyPkg, package=/path/to/MyPkg, package_name="MyPkg")
2. julia_eval_code       (session_id=..., code="using MyPkg; check()")
3. edit src/..., then julia_eval_code again with the same session_id
```

The first eval pays the compile cost; later evals reuse compiled code and Revise recompiles only what you changed. A check that takes tens of seconds cold typically takes well under a second warm, so there is no reason to batch or skip checks.
I need to verify that a function still returns the right value after my change. I was going to run `julia --project -e 'using Foo; @assert foo(2) == 4'`. Fine?

It works but it is the wrong tool: it pays process startup, package load, and compilation of `foo` every time. Use a persistent session instead.

```text
julia_eval_code(session_id=<your session>, code="using Foo; @assert foo(2) == 4")
```

If no session exists yet, call `julia_create_session` once with `project` set to the package directory. Revise is loaded in that session, so the edit you just made is picked up before the code runs. Reserve fresh `julia` processes for Pkg operations, pinned benchmarks, and the final `Pkg.test()` gate before a commit.
Is it really worth keeping a Julia session alive? A fresh `julia` process starts in under a second.

Startup of the bare runtime is fast; what is slow is everything after it: loading packages and compiling methods for the concrete argument types you use. You can see the split directly:

```text
julia --project -e 'using MyPkg'                 # load cost, every process
julia --project -e '@time MyPkg.solve(x)'        # first call: reports "% compilation time"
```

In a persistent session both costs are paid once. Measure it on your own package: time a cold `julia --project -e '...'` check against the same code in a second `julia_eval_code` call; the gap is usually one to three orders of magnitude, and it grows with package size.
Misconception check: "Julia is slow to iterate with because every edit recompiles the whole package."

That is not what happens. Compilation is per method specialization and per process. In a long-lived session with Revise, an edit re-evaluates only the changed definitions, and only the specializations of those methods (and anything that inlined them) are recompiled on their next call. Everything else stays compiled.

The slow loop comes from starting a new process per check, which throws all compiled code away. Keep the session, and iteration cost drops to the cost of the methods you touched.
How do I start a Julia session I can reuse across tool calls in this environment?

Call `julia_create_session`. Useful parameters:

- `project`: absolute path of the project to activate.
- `package` and `package_name`: the package under development, so Revise tracks it.
- `use_test_env`: activate the package's test environment.
- `julia_cmd`: path to a specific Julia executable, to pin a version.

It returns a `session_id`. Pass it to `julia_eval_code`, `julia_profile_code`, and `julia_get_session_variables`. Variables, loaded packages, and compiled code persist between calls. The response echoes the resolved environment; `julia_list_sessions` shows it again later.
My `julia_eval_code` call returned `status: "error"`. Did the tool break?

No. A Julia exception inside your code comes back as a normal result with `status: "error"`, carrying the message and backtrace. The value, captured output, and error status are separate fields. Read the message and stack trace, fix the code or the source, and call `julia_eval_code` again in the same session. Do not kill the session over an exception; the process is still alive and still warm.
My session state seems messy. Should I kill it and start clean?

No. Killing the process discards every compiled method, so the next call recompiles everything. That is the exact cost the session exists to avoid. There is also no restart tool: `julia_kill_session` followed by `julia_create_session` is a full cold start.

Instead, fix the specific problem:

- stale or conflicting global: re-assign it, or evaluate in a fresh `module Scratch ... end`.
- confusing method table: inspect it with `methods(f)` and `which(f, Tuple{Int})`.
- source edits not visible: see whether the file parses (`julia_get_diagnostics`) before suspecting the session.

Recreate a session only for things Revise cannot apply, such as a changed compile-time preference.
A session died and I need another one with the same setup. What do I pass?

There is no restart tool. Call `julia_list_sessions`: it reports each session's environment (project, package, package name, Julia command, thread count, extra args, test-env flag). Then call `julia_create_session` with those same values. The new process starts cold, so expect the first eval to pay load and compile cost again.

If creation fails repeatedly with "has died", check machine memory before suspecting the server; idle worker processes left from earlier test runs can exhaust it.
I'm thinking of calling `julia_kill_session` before every task so each task starts from a known state. Good idea?

It trades a reproducibility gain you can get more cheaply for a large latency cost. Each kill throws away all compiled code and loaded packages.

Cheaper ways to get a known state in a live session:

```julia
module Scratch
    f(x) = x + 1
    @assert f(1) == 2
end
```

A throwaway module keeps new globals out of `Main`. For the reproducibility check that matters, run the full `Pkg.test()` once in a fresh process before committing; that gate catches state the warm session hides.
I edited a function body in src/solver.jl and ran my check in the Julia session. Do I need to reload the package?

No. Revise is loaded in the session and runs before each `julia_eval_code`, so the edit is applied automatically if the file belongs to the session's project (the package you passed as `project`/`package`).

Workflow:

1. Edit `src/solver.jl`.
2. `julia_eval_code` with the check. Do not call `using` again or `include` the file.
3. If the result looks impossible, confirm the file parses with `julia_get_diagnostics` (after `julia_set_workspace_folders`) before suspecting Julia.
What files does Revise track?

Two groups:

- Source files of packages in the active project that were loaded with `using`/`import` after Revise was loaded.
- Scripts you loaded with `includet("file.jl")`.

Plain `include("file.jl")` is not tracked, so edits to that file are invisible until you include it again. Code you pass directly to `julia_eval_code` is evaluated fresh every call and needs no tracking.
I pull a helper script into my session with `include("scratch/helpers.jl")` and my edits to it have no effect. Why?

`include` evaluates the file once; Revise does not watch it. Use `includet`, which includes the file and registers it for tracking:

```julia
# partial
using Revise
includet("scratch/helpers.jl")   # edits to helpers.jl are now picked up
```

I checked this with two scripts edited after loading, one via `include` and one via `includet`: after `Revise.revise()` the `includet` one reported the new definition and the `include` one still returned the old value.
Do I need `includet` for the code I send to `julia_eval_code`?

No. Each call evaluates the code you send as-is, so a changed snippet runs as written. `includet` matters only for files on disk that you load into the session with a file path and expect to edit afterwards. Package source under the session's project needs neither.
In a plain REPL I ran `using MyPkg` and afterwards `using Revise`. Edits to MyPkg are not applied. Why?

Revise can only track packages that load after it. It hooks the package-loading machinery when it is loaded, so a package loaded earlier is invisible to it. Start with `using Revise`, then `using MyPkg`.

I reproduced this: with the order reversed, I edited a function's return string and called `Revise.revise()`; the function still returned the original value. In the JuliaMCP session Revise is loaded at startup, so the order is already right there.
My test passes in the warm session but I'm unsure the file on disk is what ran. What is the failure mode here?

Staleness: testing code that no longer exists on disk, or never executing the code you think you changed. The result is not slow, it is wrong, and it can look plausible.

Controlled check: the same edit in a process with Revise gives the new behavior, and in a process without Revise silently keeps the old behavior. So when a result looks impossible, suspect staleness first:

1. Confirm the edited file parses (`julia_get_diagnostics`).
2. Print something that can only come from the new code, such as a changed string.
3. Check `which(f, Tuple{Int})` to see the file and line the method came from.
4. Before commit, run the full suite once in a fresh process.
I introduced a syntax error in the package source, then called `julia_eval_code`. It returned status success and the old behavior. How is that possible?

Revise cannot apply a file that does not parse, so the previously loaded definitions stay in place. In my test, the eval after saving a file with an unterminated string returned the old value with `status: "success"` and empty output; after fixing the file, the next eval returned the new value with no restart.

A success status therefore does not prove your latest edit ran. After any edit that might not parse, check statically first: `julia_set_workspace_folders` once, then `julia_get_diagnostics` on the file. It parses and lints without evaluating anything.
Can I use `julia_get_diagnostics` instead of running the code to see if my edit is syntactically fine?

Yes. It analyzes the source statically (parse errors and lint warnings) without compiling or executing anything, so it costs less than an evaluation. Call `julia_set_workspace_folders` with your project folder first; the diagnostics, format, and test-item tools fail until you do. Checks that depend on the environment, such as unresolved imports, need `wait_for_ready: true`.

It cannot tell you that the code computes the right thing; for that, evaluate in the session.
Which Julia versions let Revise apply a changed `struct` definition without restarting?

Julia 1.12 and later. I tested a package whose struct gained a field, edited on disk, then `Revise.revise(throw=true)`:

- 1.10.12 and 1.11.9: error `invalid redefinition of constant RevDemo.Pt`.
- 1.12.7 and 1.13.2: the redefinition applied and `fieldnames` showed the new field.

So on 1.12+ a warm session survives struct edits. On 1.10 or 1.11 you must create a new session after changing a struct. Objects constructed before the edit keep the old type; construct fresh ones after.
I edited a struct in my package to add a field. On Julia 1.10, Revise prints `invalid redefinition of constant`. What now?

That is Julia 1.10 (and 1.11) refusing to redefine a type; the limitation was lifted in 1.12. Options:

1. Call `julia_kill_session`, then `julia_create_session` with the same environment (from `julia_list_sessions`). This is one of the few legitimate reasons to recreate a session.
2. Upgrade the session to Julia 1.12+ by passing `julia_cmd` to `julia_create_session`.

Until the session is rebuilt, Revise has stopped applying later edits that depend on that definition, so do not trust results from it.
After I redefine a struct under Revise on 1.13, do existing objects update?

No. An object built before the edit is an instance of the old type, which still exists. Methods dispatching on the new type will not accept it. Rebuild such objects after the edit:

```text
julia_eval_code: p = Pt(-2.0, 1.0)   # constructed after the change, uses the new definition
```

If a variable in the session holds an old instance, reassign it.
I changed a macro definition under Revise, but functions that use the macro show the old behavior. Bug?

Expected. A macro is expanded when the function that uses it is defined. Revise re-evaluates the macro, but callers keep the old expansion until their own definitions are re-evaluated. In a test, editing `macro m(); 1; end` to return 2 left `usem() = @m()` returning 1, while a changed plain function was picked up.

Touch each caller (any edit to its definition makes Revise re-evaluate it), or call `Revise.revise(MyPkg)`, which re-evaluates every definition of the module (the docstring names propagating an updated macro as its use). That invalidates compiled code depending on the module, so expect recompilation on the next calls.
Do I need a new session if I change a `const` in my package?

Not on Julia 1.12 or later. I edited `const K = 1` to `const K = 2` in a tracked package file, ran `Revise.revise()`, and a function reading `K` returned 2 on 1.12.7 and 1.13.2.

On 1.10.12 and 1.11.9 the same edit printed `WARNING: redefinition of constant ... This may fail, cause incorrect answers`, and the function that had already been compiled with the old value still returned 1. That is silent staleness: on those versions, create a new session after changing a `const`. Version-check before relying on live redefinition:

```julia
VERSION >= v"1.12"
```
I changed a preference that my package reads in a module-level `const`, and the value in my warm session didn't change. Why?

Compile-time preferences are baked into the package at precompile time. A module-level `const MODE = @load_preference("mode", "a")` is evaluated when the package is precompiled; changing the preference later does not change the loaded value in a running process.

I tested it: after `set_preferences!(PrefDemo, "mode" => "b"; force=true)`, the running process still reported `"a"`, and a new process loaded the package (triggering recompilation) and reported `"b"`. So after changing such a preference, kill the session and create a new one; this is a case Revise cannot handle. Read a preference inside a function (`@load_preference` is meant for compile time; use `load_preference` at run time) if you need it to change live.
What does "world age" mean in practice? I get `method too new to be called`.
I generate a function with `eval` inside a loop and call it right after; it fails with a MethodError. How do I fix it?
What is the 1.12 warning "Detected access to binding in a world prior to its definition world" telling me?

Since Julia 1.12, global bindings are world-aged too. Reading a global that was created after your running code started now warns (and is slated to become an error). The hint in the message is the fix: wrap the access in `Base.invokelatest`. You mostly see it in code that `eval`s definitions and uses them within the same function. Rewrite to avoid runtime `eval`, or use `invokelatest` at the access point.
Why does `@time f(x)` show a huge time the first call and almost nothing the second?

The first call compiles `f` for the argument types; the second reuses the compiled code. `@time` prints the share of time spent compiling:

```julia
function mysum(xs)
    s = zero(eltype(xs))
    for x in xs
        s += x
    end
    return s
end
a = collect(1:1000)
@time mysum(a)    # includes "% compilation time"
@time mysum(a)    # no compilation, tiny time
b = rand(1000)
@time mysum(b)            # new element type: compiles again
```

A new concrete argument type compiles again, so time each type you care about after its own warm-up call. Reported first-call time is not the algorithm's run time.
I benchmarked my function with `@time` once and got 0.4 s. Is that its speed?

Probably not; a single first-call `@time` mostly measures compilation. Warm up, then use a benchmarking tool that repeats and reports a median:

```julia
using BenchmarkTools
x = rand(1000)
mysum(xs) = sum(xs)
mysum(x)                 # warm-up call compiles
@btime mysum($x)         # interpolate globals with $
```

Check the `@time` line for "% compilation time": if it is large, the number is not run time. For mutating kernels use `setup=` to give each sample fresh input, for example `@benchmark mutate!(y) setup=(y = copy($x))`.
Why interpolate with `$x` in `@btime mysum($x)`?

Without `$`, the benchmark treats `x` as a non-constant global, which adds type-instability overhead that is not part of `mysum`. `$x` splices the value in so the call is measured as if its argument were a local. Always interpolate globals in BenchmarkTools macros.
Do I need to warm up when using `julia_profile_code`?

Yes. Evaluate the code once with `julia_eval_code` first, then profile it. Otherwise the samples are dominated by compilation of your function and the profiler, not the work you want to see.

```text
1. julia_eval_code     (code="run_workload()")      # compiles
2. julia_profile_code  (code="run_workload()")      # samples CPU
```

The same tool can sample allocations instead of CPU with `kind="alloc"`. Use the same session for both calls, since a new session would be cold again.
Why is the profile of my function mostly time in the compiler?

You profiled the first call. The profiler sampled type inference and codegen for your function, not its steady-state work. Call the function once in the session so it is compiled, then profile again; the compiler frames should disappear. If they stay, something is being recompiled each call (for example a new closure or a type that changes every time) and that is itself the finding.
What is PrecompileTools for?

It lets a package run a representative workload while it precompiles so the resulting native code is cached in the package image. Users then pay no compile cost on their first call of those methods.

```julia
# partial
module MyPkg
using PrecompileTools

mysum(xs) = sum(xs)

@compile_workload begin
    mysum(collect(1:10))
end
end
```

I measured this: the first call of a function covered by the workload took microseconds in a new process, versus several milliseconds of compilation when the workload was removed. Only the concrete signatures the workload exercises are cached; a call with a different element type still compiles.
I added a `@compile_workload` block but the first call is still slow for `Float32` input. Why?

The workload cached specializations only for the types it called. If it ran `mysum(collect(1:10))`, only the `Vector{Int}` method instance is cached; `Vector{Float32}` is a different specialization and compiles on first use. Add the types users will actually pass:

```julia
# partial
@compile_workload begin
    mysum(collect(1:10))
    mysum(rand(Float32, 10))
    mysum(rand(10))
end
```

Each extra signature increases precompile time and image size, so cover the common ones, not every combination.
Should I put `@compile_workload` calls in a script I run in my session to warm it up?

No. `@compile_workload` is for package source: it executes during precompilation and caches the result in the package image. In a session you just call the function once (with realistic argument types) and it stays compiled for the life of the process. Use PrecompileTools to make a package's first-call latency low for all its users; use a warm-up call to make your own session fast.
What is an invalidation in Julia?

Defining a new method can make previously compiled code wrong, because a call that used to resolve to one method might now resolve to a more specific one. Julia then invalidates (discards) the compiled code that depended on the old dispatch, and it is recompiled on next use.

Demonstration with `@time`, which labels such compilation as recompilation:

```julia
hh(x) = 1
callit(xs) = sum(hh(x) for x in xs)
a = collect(1:1000)
callit(a)
@time callit(a)       # compiled, fast
hh(x::Int) = 2        # more specific method invalidates callit's compiled code
@time callit(a)       # "% compilation time: 100% of which was recompilation"
@time callit(a)       # fast again
```

Invalidations matter for latency because loading a package that adds methods can invalidate code compiled by others, increasing time to first call.
How can I find out which method definition invalidated my compiled code?

Use SnoopCompile. Load SnoopCompileCore first, record invalidations around the code that defines methods, then analyze:

```julia
# partial
using SnoopCompileCore
f(x) = 1
g(xs) = sum(f(x) for x in xs)
g([1, 2])
invs = @snoop_invalidations (Core.eval(Main, :(f(x::Int) = 2)))
using SnoopCompile
trees = invalidation_trees(invs)
```

In my run, `trees` held one entry: inserting `f(x::Int64)` invalidated a backedge for `f(::Int64)` with 16 children. The tree tells you which new method caused which compiled instances to be dropped. For real packages, wrap `using TheDependency` in `@snoop_invalidations`.
Why does SnoopCompile need `using SnoopCompileCore` before the code I want to analyze?

SnoopCompileCore is the small package that records data; it has almost no dependencies, so loading it does not itself invalidate or compile much. SnoopCompile is the heavier analysis package. The pattern is: load the light recorder, run the code under `@snoop_invalidations`, and only then load SnoopCompile to analyze the saved data. Loading the heavy package first would add its own methods and perturb the thing you are measuring.
My long benchmark script redirected to a file shows no output until it finishes. Is it hung?

Probably not. Julia flushes stdout line by line only when it is a terminal. Redirected to a file or pipe, it is block-buffered, so output appears when the buffer fills or the process exits. I tested a loop printing every 2 seconds and checked the file at 4 seconds:

```text
println(i)                           0 lines visible
println(i); flush(stdout)            2 lines visible
println(stderr, i)                   0 lines visible (stderr is buffered too)
println(stderr, i); flush(stderr)    2 lines
@info i                              0 lines
```

Add an explicit flush after progress prints:

```julia
for i in 1:3
    println("step ", i)
    flush(stdout)
end
```
I can't edit the script. Can I still get live output when redirecting?

Run it under a pseudo-terminal so Julia sees a TTY and line-buffers:

```text
script -qec "julia --project=bench bench/run.jl" /dev/null > progress.log
```

In my test this showed the lines as they were printed. Do not use `stdbuf -oL julia ...`: it exits successfully and changes nothing, because Julia does its own I/O through libuv rather than libc stdio, which is what `stdbuf` adjusts.
Will `stdbuf -oL julia script.jl > log.txt` make output appear line by line?

No. I tested it with a loop that prints every 2 seconds: after 4 seconds the log had 0 lines, the same as with no wrapper. `stdbuf` works by preloading a library that changes libc stdio buffering; Julia's stdout goes through libuv and is unaffected. Use `flush(stdout)` in the code, or run under `script -qec "julia ..." /dev/null` to give it a pty.
Does `@info` flush so I can see progress in a redirected log?

No. `@info` and `@warn` write to stderr through a buffered stream, so with redirection they appear late too. In my test, five `@info` calls spaced 2 seconds apart left the file empty at 4 seconds. Follow a log message with `flush(stderr)`, or print with `println` and `flush(stdout)` for progress you want to watch.
I'll start the 20-minute benchmark in the background and check on it later.

Run it in the foreground with a generous timeout instead. A command you background and then wait on can leave you stuck: if the completion notification goes to a different party than the one waiting, the waiter never gets it, and the work finishes unreported.

```text
Bash(command="julia --project=bench bench/run.jl", timeout=900000)
```

If you must background it, poll for completion within the same turn:

```text
until grep -q DONE out.log; do sleep 5; done
```

Never end your turn waiting for a background process. Pair the foreground run with `flush(stdout)` in the script so you can see progress if the tool streams output.
The first `julia_eval_code` call in a new session timed out while loading my package. What happened?

Probably the package (or a heavy dependency) was not precompiled yet, and the first load precompiled it, which can take minutes. Pay that once, deliberately, before creating the session:

```text
julia --project=/path/to/MyPkg -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.precompile()'
```

Run it in the foreground with a long timeout. Then `julia_create_session`. You can also pass `timeout` to `julia_eval_code` to bound a call. A timeout during first load is not a sign that the package is broken.
Should Pkg operations also go through the warm session?

Cold `julia` is appropriate for exactly three things: Pkg operations on environments (add, resolve, instantiate, precompile), benchmarks that must run in a pinned clean process, and the final full-suite `Pkg.test()` before a commit. Everything else, including iteration, profiling, and "does this still work", belongs in the warm session. The cold final test also catches world-age and stale-definition problems that a long-lived session can mask.
Why is a final `Pkg.test()` still needed if every check passes in my warm session?

A long-lived session accumulates state: global variables, method definitions from earlier experiments, and compiled code that Revise left patched. A test can pass because a leftover definition is present, or because a stale method masks a missing one. `Pkg.test()` runs in a new process with a clean environment, so it runs exactly what is on disk. Use filtered tests while iterating and run the full cold suite as the gate before committing.
My benchmark probe measured the "unfixed" path but showed the fix's speed. The session had been used for an earlier experiment. What's going on?

The experiment defined the method you later believed absent, and a persistent session keeps method definitions. The "before" run silently used the fixed path. Before measuring the absence of a method, assert which method runs:

```julia
f(x) = 1
f(x::Int) = 2
which(f, Tuple{Int})
```

`which` prints the method that a call with that signature resolves to. If it is not the fallback you expect, remove the definition by recreating the session (this is a justified kill) or evaluate the probe in a fresh `module`. Print `methods(f)` in the script's header so the output records the state.
In my session I get "cannot define function f; it already has a value". My code worked earlier.

An earlier call assigned a variable named `f` in `Main`, and a function definition cannot reuse that name. In a script that persists globals, an old `f = ...` is enough:

```julia
f = 1
try
    Core.eval(Main, :(f(x) = x))
catch e
    println(sprint(showerror, e))
end
```

Output: `cannot define function f; it already has a value`. Rename the function or the variable, or evaluate the definition in a fresh module. Sessions keep globals across calls, so name collisions with earlier experiments are common; `julia_get_session_variables` lists what is defined.
How can I list what's in my session's global scope?

Call `julia_get_session_variables` with the `session_id`. It shows the variables defined in the session, which helps when a name collision or a leftover from an earlier experiment is changing behavior. To remove an unwanted binding without killing the session, shadow it in a fresh module for the experiment instead, since Julia cannot unassign a global in `Main`.
My timings of the same BLAS-using function vary wildly between runs, and a single-threaded version looks 2x slower than expected.

Pin the BLAS thread count before any timing. Julia's OpenBLAS is multithreaded by default and its idle threads spin-wait, which interferes with single-threaded code you measure and with the BLAS call itself.

```julia
using LinearAlgebra
BLAS.set_num_threads(1)
BLAS.get_num_threads()   # 1
```

Print `BLAS.get_num_threads()` next to your timing results. In a published case, a pure-Julia factorization at n=800 timed more than twice slower with the BLAS threads live than with them pinned, and the unpinned run reversed the conclusion of the comparison. Pin first, measure second.
Do I need to set BLAS threads again in each script if I use a persistent session?

Yes, set it at the top of every timing script. The setting persists in the session process, so an earlier benchmark that pinned one thread leaves it at one for later probes, and a different setup may leave it at eight. That produces mutually contradictory numbers for the same kernel with no code change. Make the thread count explicit and report it:

```julia
using LinearAlgebra
BLAS.set_num_threads(1)
println("BLAS threads = ", BLAS.get_num_threads())
```
Two benchmark runs of identical code disagree by 7x. Where do I look first?

At environment state before the code: BLAS thread count, other running Julia processes, and memory pressure. A ratio near the core count (for example about 8x on an 8-core machine) is the tell for BLAS threading. Check:

```julia
using LinearAlgebra
BLAS.get_num_threads()
Threads.nthreads()
```

and list processes:

```text
ps -eo pid,etime,rss,args | grep '[j]ulia'
```

Old Julia processes holding gigabytes, or a stranded test run, can make timings unstable. Fix the environment, rerun, and only then reason about the code. Do not name a mechanism ("memory bound") until you have measured.
How do I find leftover Julia processes that may be skewing benchmarks or eating memory?

List them with age and resident memory:

```text
ps -eo pid,etime,rss,args | grep '[j]ulia'
ps -eo rss,args | grep -i '[j]ulia' | awk '{s+=$1} END {print s/1048576" GB"}'
```

Age is the tell: processes much older than your current work are strays. Kill by explicit PID, not `pkill -f julia`, because the pattern also matches the shell command that contains it. Keep the language server, the MCP server for your live sessions, and any Julia whose parent is your own shell. Idle test workers that respawn on demand are safe to remove.
My test run was cancelled weirdly and now later runs hang. I'm going to `kill -9` the workers.

Cancel the run first, then clean up. Killing workers while a run is in flight leaves the run unfinished, so its worker pool is never released and the processes sit holding memory.

```text
1. julia_list_testruns          # find any run still "running"
2. julia_cancel_testrun         # cancel it
3. julia_list_test_processes    # see remaining workers
4. julia_terminate_test_process # per id, for strays
```

Only after that, if processes remain, kill them by explicit PID. Also pass `max_workers` to `julia_run_testitems` (1 when iterating on one item), since the default launches several full Julia processes.
Why do my Julia processes keep piling up as I run test items repeatedly?

Test workers are returned to a pool after a run rather than terminated, so they stay resident by design: a warm worker skips package load next time. `max_workers` limits one run's concurrency, not the total across runs, so successive runs can add workers. Memory climbs over a session.

Manage it explicitly: pass `max_workers=1` for single-item iteration, check `julia_list_test_processes` between runs, and `julia_terminate_test_process` the ones you no longer need (after `julia_cancel_testrun` if a run is active).
How do I run one test item quickly instead of the whole suite?

Use the test-item tools instead of `Pkg.test()`:

```text
1. julia_set_workspace_folders (folders=[<project dir>])
2. julia_list_testitems        -> ids like MyPkg@a1b2c3d4/test/parsing_tests.jl::parse basics
3. julia_run_testitems         (items=[<id>], max_workers=1)
4. julia_get_testitem_detail   for failures
5. julia_rerun_failed          after an edit
```

Workers stay alive between runs and hot-reload edits via Revise, so iteration on one item takes a fraction of a second warm versus a full cold suite. Run the whole suite cold only as a gate before commit.
Should I disable Revise to make my session faster?

No. Revise is what lets edits take effect without restarting. Without it, edits are silently ignored: the same edit applied in a process with Revise gave the new result, and without Revise the old result, with no error. Fast and stale is the failure to avoid.
What can't Revise do?

It cannot apply everything. From testing and its documented scope:

- Edits that do not parse: the old definitions stay and the result looks like success.
- Macro changes: callers keep the old expansion until re-evaluated.
- Compile-time values baked into a package image, such as `@load_preference` in a module-level `const`: need a new process.
- Julia 1.10/1.11: struct redefinition errors and `const` changes leave stale values; Julia 1.12+ applies both.
- Files loaded with plain `include`, or packages loaded before Revise: untracked.

Everything else, such as method bodies and new methods in tracked files, applies on the next `julia_eval_code`.
Is it fine to run `Pkg.add` from inside my warm session?

You can, but it modifies the active environment and can trigger precompilation inside the session process, with long, possibly timed-out calls. Prefer a cold `julia --project=<env> -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.add("Foo")'` in the foreground, then a new `using Foo` in the session. Project-file edits are authored changes to the environment, not code, and are a legitimate use of a cold process.
I changed a function in a package that my project depends on but did not develop. My session doesn't pick it up.

Revise tracks packages that you load from a source directory that it can watch, normally your project's own package or one added with `Pkg.develop`. A registered dependency installed read-only in the depot is not meant to be edited. Use `Pkg.develop(path=...)` (cold process) to point the project at the local copy, create a session, and Revise will track that copy. For one-off experiments, define the replacement method in a `julia_eval_code` snippet; code passed to eval takes effect immediately.
Explain how time to first call splits between "loading" and "compiling".

Two separate costs:

- Loading (`using Foo`): reading the package image from disk, and running `__init__`. Precompilation makes this fast; the first load after a source change or version bump precompiles and is slow.
- Compiling: the first call of a function with new argument types runs inference and codegen. A `@compile_workload` in the package moves some of this into the package image.

Measure separately:

```julia
@time using LinearAlgebra   # load
A = rand(50, 50)
@time A * A                 # first call may include compilation
@time A * A
```

Use a warm session so you pay both only once.
What does "100% of which was recompilation" in the `@time` output mean?

Of the time spent compiling, all of it was recompiling a method instance that had been compiled before and was then invalidated. It means something you defined (or loaded) after the first compile changed method dispatch for that code. Look for new, more specific methods defined between the two calls. In a session, repeated `hh(x::Int) = 2` style definitions on a function that others call is a typical source. SnoopCompile's `invalidation_trees` identifies the culprit method.
Should I call `GC.gc()` or tune GC flags to stabilize my benchmarks?

No. If garbage collection pauses distort timing, eliminate the allocation that triggers it. Check with `@time` or `@allocated` (second call, after warm-up) and make the hot path allocation-free. GC tuning hides the cause and changes the program being measured.

Review this timing code:

```julia
function work(n)
    s = 0.0
    for i in 1:n
        s += sqrt(i)
    end
    return s
end
t = @elapsed work(10^7)
println("work takes ", t, " s")
```

The measurement includes compilation of `work(::Int)`, because it is the first call, and it times a global-scope expression once. Warm up, then measure repeatedly and report a median:

```julia
using BenchmarkTools
function work(n)
    s = 0.0
    for i in 1:n
        s += sqrt(i)
    end
    return s
end
work(10)                       # compiles for Int
b = @benchmark work($(10^7))
println("median: ", median(b).time / 1e6, " ms")
```

`$(10^7)` interpolates the argument so it is not a global lookup. Keep `s = 0.0`: the accumulator type is stable (`Float64`).

This benchmark warms up with an Int and then times a Float64 call. Anything wrong?

```julia
using BenchmarkTools
scale(x) = 2 * x + 1
scale(1)
@btime scale($(1.5))
```

`@btime` runs many samples and takes the minimum, so compilation does not leak into its number here, but the warm-up did not warm the case you measure. That matters for `@time` and for any single-shot timer, where the `Float64` call would still compile. Warm up with the same concrete types you time:

```julia
using BenchmarkTools
scale(x) = 2 * x + 1
x = 1.5
scale(x)
@btime scale($x)
```

Also note that a trivial function like this may be constant-folded or inlined away, so the number can reflect the benchmark harness, not the function.

Fix this script that prints progress from a long computation and is run with output redirected to a log file:

```julia
for n in (100, 200, 400, 800)
    t = @elapsed sum(abs2, rand(n, n))
    println("n=", n, " t=", t)
end
```

Output goes to a block-buffered stream when redirected, so nothing appears in the log until the buffer fills or the process exits. Flush after each progress line:

```julia
for n in (100, 200, 400, 800)
    t = @elapsed sum(abs2, rand(n, n))
    println("n=", n, " t=", t)
    flush(stdout)
end
```

The first iteration's `t` also includes compilation; call `sum(abs2, rand(2, 2))` once before the loop if you need the numbers to be comparable.

Why does this logging line not show up in my log until the program ends?

```julia
@info "finished stage" stage=3
```

`@info` writes to `stderr`, and when stderr is redirected to a file or pipe Julia buffers it. Flush explicitly after the message:

```julia
@info "finished stage" stage=3
flush(stderr)
```

Redirecting both streams (`> log 2>&1`) does not change this. For code you cannot edit, run it under a pseudo-terminal: `script -qec "julia --project run.jl" /dev/null`.

The result depends on how many OpenBLAS threads are active, because Julia's BLAS is multithreaded by default and idle BLAS threads spin-wait. If you want to compare against single-threaded code, or want reproducible numbers, pin first and print the setting:

```julia
using LinearAlgebra, BenchmarkTools
BLAS.set_num_threads(1)
println("BLAS threads: ", BLAS.get_num_threads())
A = rand(800, 800)
B = A'A + 800I
@btime cholesky($B);
```

Also build `B` outside the timed expression so you time the factorization, not the matrix product. Report the thread count with the result.

This loop checks each of my 5 edits by launching Julia. Rewrite it to avoid the repeated cost.

```text
for f in a b c d e
    julia --project -e "using MyPkg; MyPkg.check(\"$f\")"
end
```

That is five process starts, five package loads, and five rounds of compilation. Do the loop inside one Julia process, in a persistent session:

```julia
# partial
using MyPkg
for f in ("a", "b", "c", "d", "e")
    MyPkg.check(f)
end
```

Send it through `julia_eval_code` to a session created with `julia_create_session` on the project. The first iteration compiles; the remaining iterations reuse that work.

Review this REPL setup. My edits are not picked up:

```julia
# partial
using MyPkg
using Revise
MyPkg.run()
```

Revise is loaded after the package, so it never started tracking `MyPkg`. Load Revise first:

```julia
# partial
using Revise
using MyPkg
MyPkg.run()
```

I confirmed that with the order reversed an edited return value stayed at its original value after `Revise.revise()`. In a JuliaMCP session Revise is already loaded at startup, so this only bites in a hand-started REPL or script.

Fix: my helper script edits don't take effect.

```julia
# partial
using Revise
include("scratch/probe.jl")
probe()
```

Replace `include` with `includet` so Revise tracks the file:

```julia
# partial
using Revise
includet("scratch/probe.jl")
probe()
```

After editing `probe.jl`, the next evaluation (or `Revise.revise()`) applies the change. Alternatively paste the probe code directly into `julia_eval_code`; code sent there is evaluated fresh each time and needs no tracking.

`make_and_call` is already running in an older world than the new `helper` method, so the call fails ("method too new to be called"). Call through `invokelatest`, or avoid `eval` altogether:

```julia
function make_and_call(v)
    helper = () -> v + 1
    return helper()
end
make_and_call(1)
```

If you really need generated global functions, keep the `@eval` but call with `Base.invokelatest(helper)`. The closure version is also faster and does not define anything global.

Review this module. It reads a setting at precompile time but I toggle it during a session.

```julia
# partial
module Tuned
using Preferences
const BACKEND = @load_preference("backend", "generic")
backend() = BACKEND
end
```

`const BACKEND = @load_preference(...)` is evaluated while the package precompiles, and the value is baked in. Changing the preference in a running session has no effect; a new process is needed (and triggers recompilation). That is acceptable if the value selects code at compile time, and you should then recreate the session after each change.

If the value must change live, read it when called:

```julia
# partial
module Tuned
using Preferences
backend() = load_preference(@__MODULE__, "backend", "generic")
end
```

Run-time reads cost a lookup per call, so cache the result in a `Ref` if it is on a hot path.

Spot the problem in this benchmark script's global:

```julia
using BenchmarkTools
data = rand(10_000)
@btime sum(data)
```

`data` is a non-constant global, so the benchmark includes dynamic-lookup overhead that is not part of `sum`. Interpolate it:

```julia
using BenchmarkTools
data = rand(10_000)
@btime sum($data)
```

Julia measures the call as if `data` were a local. Without `$` the reported time and allocations are inflated; the difference is small only when the work per call is large.

I measured these two versions with `@time` once each, B looks 100x faster. Is B better?

```julia
using LinearAlgebra
A = rand(200, 200)
@time A * A          # version A
@time mul!(similar(A), A, A)   # version B
```

You cannot tell. Both lines are first calls in the process; each may include compile time, and the order matters because the first call to `*` may compile shared code that the second call then reuses. Warm both, then compare medians:

```julia
using LinearAlgebra, BenchmarkTools
BLAS.set_num_threads(1)
A = rand(200, 200)
C = similar(A)
A * A; mul!(C, A, A)         # warm both paths
@btime $A * $A
@btime mul!($C, $A, $A)
```

Expect version B to differ mainly by avoiding the output allocation. State the BLAS thread count when you report numbers.

Fix this profiling request:

```text
julia_profile_code(session_id=S, code="solve(problem)")
```
as the first call in a new session.

The first run of `solve` compiles, so the profile is dominated by inference and codegen. Warm it first, in the same session:

```text
1. julia_eval_code    (session_id=S, code="solve(problem)")
2. julia_profile_code (session_id=S, code="solve(problem)")
```

For allocation hot spots use the allocation variant (`kind="alloc"`) after the same warm-up. If the compiler frames persist after warm-up, the code is being recompiled each call, and that is the thing to fix.
I edited src/solver.jl and the test still shows the old result. What do I do, in order?

```text
1. julia_set_workspace_folders (once) then julia_get_diagnostics on src/solver.jl
      -> confirms the edited file parses; a syntax error makes Revise keep old code silently
2. julia_eval_code: which(solve, Tuple{typeof(problem)})
      -> shows the file and line of the method actually in use
3. julia_eval_code: print a value only the new code can produce
4. If the session was created before the file was part of the project, or on Julia 1.10/1.11 after a struct/const edit:
      julia_list_sessions, julia_kill_session, julia_create_session with the same environment
5. Before commit: one cold Pkg.test() in a fresh process
```

Do step 4 last; most stale results come from step 1.
I ran my test item in the warm session and it passed, but I suspect it ran old code.

Check what the session actually loaded: evaluate `which(f, Tuple{Int})` for the function under test and compare the reported line with your edit. Also run `julia_get_diagnostics` on the edited file to make sure it parses; an unparseable file leaves old definitions in place and the run still reports success.
which says line 42, and the file has it at line 57 now.

Then Revise did not apply your latest edit. Likely causes, in order:

1. The file has a syntax error, so Revise skipped it. Run `julia_get_diagnostics` and fix it; the next `julia_eval_code` applies the fix.
2. The file is outside the session's tracked project, or was loaded with plain `include`. Load it with `includet` or move the code under the project's `src/`.
3. The session was created on Julia 1.10/1.11 and the edit changed a struct or `const`; recreate it (or use 1.12+).

After the fix, `which` should report line 57.
Julia session creation keeps failing with "has died". The server looks broken.

Check memory before suspecting the server. Leftover Julia processes (test workers from earlier runs, sessions from abandoned work) can use gigabytes each and exhaust RAM, and creation then fails every time.

```text
ps -eo pid,etime,rss,args | grep '[j]ulia'
```

Then, in order: `julia_list_testruns` and `julia_cancel_testrun` for runs stuck in "running"; `julia_list_test_processes` and `julia_terminate_test_process` per id; for processes left by dead sessions, kill by explicit PID. Retry `julia_create_session`; it should recover once memory is free.
I need to run the full test suite of a heavy package. Which call do I make?

`julia_run_testitems` with `max_workers` set explicitly: the default launches several full Julia processes, each loading the package. Use 1 for one item or a handful, 2 to 4 for a full suite when wall-clock matters.

```text
julia_list_testitems -> ids
julia_run_testitems (items=<ids or omit for all>, max_workers=2)
```

If the call returns `status: "running"` after `max_wait_seconds`, poll `julia_get_testrun_results` with the `testrun_id`, leaving time between polls. Do not start a second run of the same items while it is going.
It returned status running with a testrun id. Should I just wait for it to finish and end my turn?

Do not end your turn waiting. Poll within the same turn: call `julia_get_testrun_results` with the `testrun_id`; each call returns immediately, so leave a gap between calls. If it stays at "running" implausibly long, a test item is probably hanging: `julia_cancel_testrun`, then re-run with a per-item `timeout` so the hanging item is reported as errored and the rest finish.
I'm delegating a Julia task to a subagent. What should I tell it about running things?

Include these rules explicitly:

- Use the persistent session (`julia_create_session`, `julia_eval_code`) for checks; no `julia -e` per check.
- Precompile first: `julia --project=<abs path> -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.precompile()'` in the foreground, before creating the session.
- Run long commands in the foreground with a generous timeout; never background a command and then end the turn waiting for it, since the completion signal may not reach the subagent.
- Pass `max_workers` to `julia_run_testitems`, and do not kill sessions "to start clean".

The foreground rule is the most valuable: a subagent that backgrounds work and then waits can finish the work and never report.
Which Julia does a new session use? I need 1.10 to check an issue.

A session uses the Julia that runs the server, which is whatever the default channel of the version manager is. To pin one, pass `julia_cmd` (the path to the executable) to `julia_create_session`. For a second version, create a second session; keep both alive. Facts that may differ between versions, such as struct redefinition under Revise (works on 1.12 and later, errors on 1.10 and 1.11), are worth checking in both.
I added `include("extra.jl")` to my package module. Does the session need to be recreated?

Try the edit first. In my test on Julia 1.13.2, adding an `include("extra.jl")` line to the tracked module file made the functions in `extra.jl` available on the next `julia_eval_code`, without a restart. If an evaluation still raises `UndefVarError` after the file parses, recreate the session (`julia_list_sessions`, `julia_kill_session`, `julia_create_session` with the same environment). Do not recreate it preemptively.
I changed the signature of a function used by 40 others in my package. Do I need to restart?

No. Revise adds the new method; callers that dispatch to it recompile when next called. Run the tests that exercise the callers, which now see the new signature. Any caller you forgot to update raises a `MethodError` immediately, which is the information you want.
Julia caches compiled code on disk, so my `julia script.jl` should be fast the second time, right?

Only for packages. Precompilation caches the code of packages (and their precompile workloads) in package images. Code in your script itself, and methods it calls with new type combinations, are compiled again in every process. So a script that loads a package pays little load time on later runs but still compiles its own functions every time.

To check, run a script that defines a function and calls it under `@time`; the report shows compilation time on every run. The remedy is a long-lived session, or moving the code into a package with a `@compile_workload`.
Revise reloads everything I `include` into the REPL automatically, doesn't it?

No. It tracks packages loaded after it and files loaded with `includet`. A file loaded with `include` is evaluated once and then ignored: I edited one via `include` and one via `includet`, ran `Revise.revise()`, and only the `includet` definition changed.
Isn't world age just something that matters when I use Revise?

No. It is a core language mechanism: running code sees the methods that existed when it started, and new methods become visible to later top-level calls. You encounter it whenever code defines a method (via `eval`, `include_string`, or loading) and calls it in the same running function. Revise makes it visible more often because it adds methods to a running program; the fix, `Base.invokelatest` at the call, is the same with or without it.
Do invalidations mean I wrote a bug?

No. An invalidation is a consequence of adding a more specific method that code compiled earlier could have called. It makes the earlier compiled code stale and it is recompiled, correct but slow. Invalidations from your own definitions are routine; they hurt when a package's methods invalidate lots of compiled code in packages it merely depends on, adding to everyone's latency. SnoopCompile's `invalidation_trees` shows which method caused which invalidations, and the usual fix is to make the offending method signature less broad or add a type annotation at the call site.
Should I worry about compile time when my function is only called once?

Yes, for a one-shot call it is most of the cost: compiling and running a function once pays the full inference and codegen price. Typical advice differs by situation: in an interactive or agent loop, keep a warm session so each function compiles once; for a script that runs once, minimize the number of distinct specializations, and for a package, use `@compile_workload` so the cost is paid at precompile instead of by users.
How do I tell whether slowness in a call is compilation or the algorithm?

Call it twice and compare, and read `@time`'s compilation share:

```julia
f(xs) = sum(abs2, xs) / length(xs)
xs = rand(10_000)
@time f(xs)    # first: compile + run
@time f(xs)    # second: run only
```

If the second call is fast, the first was compilation. If the second call is also slow, profile it: `julia_eval_code` once to warm up, then `julia_profile_code`. Do not call a function slow, or name a bottleneck, before you have separated these two.
I think the slowdown is memory bandwidth. Let me write that in the report.

Not yet; that is a hypothesis. Decompose before concluding: warm the function, pin `BLAS.set_num_threads(1)` if BLAS is involved, time the full kernel and the pieces separately, vary the problem size across cache sizes, and compare to a simple copy over the same arrays. Only measured evidence belongs in the report. If you have not measured it, write "unverified hypothesis".

`@time` here measures `fill` and `sum` together, once per type, so the number mixes allocation of the vector with the reduction, and a single sample is noisy. The first call for each type can also include compilation, which `@time` reports as a compilation percentage when it is present. Build the data outside the timed expression, warm each type, and benchmark only the operation:

```julia
using BenchmarkTools
function bench()
    for x in (1, 1.0, 1f0)
        v = fill(x, 1000)
        sum(v)
        println(typeof(x), " ", median(@benchmark sum($v)).time, " ns")
    end
end
bench()
```

Time each type after its own warm-up call, and interpolate the data.
Should I put `@compile_workload` around my test code?

No. A workload belongs in the package source and should exercise the common, user-facing calls with typical argument types, because it runs during every precompile and its results are stored in the package image. Test code runs in a separate process and covers edge cases; putting it in the workload would slow precompilation for no benefit and would cache irrelevant specializations.
Does PrecompileTools make `using MyPkg` slower?

I have not measured that, and do not want to assert it. Qualitatively, the workload executes during precompilation, not at load, so it lengthens the one-time precompile; at load the package image is read from disk and may be somewhat larger. To decide for your package, measure `@time using MyPkg` (in a fresh process) with and without the workload, and also the first-call time of the covered functions.
Give me a template for a progress-printing benchmark loop that is safe to run with redirected output.

```julia
using BenchmarkTools, LinearAlgebra, Printf
BLAS.set_num_threads(1)
println("BLAS threads = ", BLAS.get_num_threads()); flush(stdout)
for n in (50, 100, 200)
    A = rand(n, n)
    A * A                              # warm-up for this size/type
    t = median(@benchmark $A * $A).time / 1e6
    @printf("n=%d median=%.3f ms\n", n, t)
    flush(stdout)
end
```

It pins BLAS threads, warms each case, reports the median, and flushes after every line so a redirected log shows progress.
I'm about to run `pkill -f julia` to clean up. OK?

Avoid it. `pkill -f` matches the full command line, which includes the shell command that launched `pkill`, so it can terminate your own shell, and it also kills sessions and servers you want to keep. List first, then kill by PID:

```text
ps -eo pid,etime,rss,args | grep '[j]ulia'
kill <pid>
```

Keep the MCP server process, the language server, and Julia processes whose parent is your terminal. For test workers, prefer `julia_terminate_test_process` after `julia_cancel_testrun`.
Two of my own measurements of the same function disagree. How do I debug?

Suspect the environment before the code. Checklist:

1. Same Julia version and thread count? `VERSION`, `Threads.nthreads()`.
2. `BLAS.get_num_threads()` identical in both?
3. Other Julia processes running (`ps -eo pid,etime,rss,args | grep '[j]ulia'`)?
4. Was the session reused? A leftover method definition or global can change which code runs: `which(f, Tuple{...})`.
5. Was each timing warmed up and taken as a median?

Record these values next to every result. Only after they match should you look at the code.
How can a warm session mask a bug that a fresh process shows?

A persistent session keeps state a fresh start would not have. Examples: a global variable defined in an earlier cell, a method defined by an experiment that the package source does not contain, or a type from before a redefinition. The code then works because of that leftover state, and fails when run in a clean process.

Defend against it with a cold full-suite run before commit, with `Pkg.test()` in a new process. That run uses only what is on disk, so it exposes missing definitions and order dependencies the session hid.
Show me the minimal workflow for editing a package function and checking it.

```text
1. julia_create_session (project=/path/to/MyPkg, package=/path/to/MyPkg, package_name="MyPkg")
2. julia_eval_code (code="using MyPkg; MyPkg.f(3)")        # pays load + compile once
3. edit src/MyPkg.jl (or any file it includes)
4. julia_eval_code (code="MyPkg.f(3)")                       # Revise applies the edit first
5. julia_get_diagnostics if the result did not change (syntax error?)
6. repeat 3-4; at the end run the cold Pkg.test() gate
```

Do not kill the session between iterations, and do not re-run `using` or `include`.
What is the difference between `julia_eval_code` with `revise=false` and the default?

By default Revise runs before the evaluation, so on-disk edits to tracked files are applied first. With `revise=false` it is skipped, so the code runs against whatever is currently loaded, even if the files on disk changed. In a control test, `revise=false` after an edit kept returning the stale result, while the default returned the new one. Leave the default on unless you deliberately want the old definitions.
My function got slow after I loaded another package in the same session.

Check whether loading it caused invalidations. Run the call under `@time` right after the load: if the output reports a compilation share with "of which was recompilation", loading the package invalidated compiled code that your function depended on.

Compare the first call after the `using` with the second call. A one-time cost on the first call after loading means invalidation plus recompile, not a permanently slower function.
It's slow every time, not just the first.

Then it is not invalidation; recompilation would disappear after the first call. Profile after a warm-up: `julia_eval_code` once, then `julia_profile_code`. Look at whether dispatch changed (a more general method now being chosen, via `which(f, Tuple{...})`) and whether allocations appear (`@time` shows them). Report measurements, not a guessed mechanism.
Do I need to call `Revise.revise()` myself before each evaluation in the session?

No. The session server runs Revise before every `julia_eval_code` (the default `revise=true`), so edits to tracked files are already applied when your code runs. A manual call is redundant. Call it yourself only to get errors surfaced: `Revise.revise(throw=true)` throws errors from a failed revision, whereas plain `revise()` only logs them.
How do I see why Revise could not apply my edit?

By default revision errors are only logged, so an eval can succeed with old code. Surface them:

```text
julia_eval_code(session_id=S, code="using Revise; Revise.revise(throw=true)", revise=false)
```

`throw=true` rethrows errors raised during revision. A file that does not parse is better caught statically with `julia_get_diagnostics`, which reports the syntax error and its location without evaluating anything.
How can I confirm which source line a method in my session comes from?

Use `which` with the argument types:

```julia
f(x::Int) = 1
f(x) = 2
which(f, Tuple{Int})       # f(x::Int64) @ Main ...
which(f, Tuple{Float64})   # f(x) @ Main ...
```

For a package function it prints the file and line. Compare that line with the edited file; a mismatch means the edit was not applied, usually because the file did not parse or is not tracked.
I'll use `Pkg.test()` for each iteration since it guarantees a clean process.

It guarantees a clean process, and that is its cost: every run starts cold, loads the package and its test environment, and compiles everything again. Use it as a gate before a commit or merge, not as the inner loop.

Inner loop: a warm session, with one test item at a time (`julia_run_testitems` with `max_workers=1`, or a plain call in `julia_eval_code`). Full suite: once, cold, when you are done.
How do I measure allocations of a function properly?

Warm it up, then measure the second call:

```julia
function addone!(y, x)
    for i in eachindex(y, x)
        y[i] = x[i] + 1
    end
    return y
end
x = rand(100); y = similar(x)
addone!(y, x)               # compile
@allocated addone!(y, x)    # 0
```

`@allocated` on the first call counts allocations made by the compiler. Put the call in a function or use `$` interpolation if you use BenchmarkTools, so globals do not add allocations.
Can I use Chairmarks instead of BenchmarkTools?

Yes. Warm up, interpolate globals, and read the median:

```julia
using Chairmarks
x = rand(1000)
sum(x)             # warm-up
b = @b sum($x)
```

`@b` returns a sample summarizing the runs. As with BenchmarkTools, benchmark the warm function with the same argument types, and pin `BLAS.set_num_threads(1)` when BLAS is involved.
Isn't it enough to run `julia --project -e 'using MyPkg'` once to know my package is OK?

It checks that the package loads and precompiles, which is only part of "OK". It does not run any function, so nothing compiles and no behavior is exercised. For behavior, call the functions and run the tests in a warm session. For the load check itself, running a cold `Pkg.precompile()` once is the right use of a cold process.
Is there a good pattern for trying alternative implementations in one session without them interfering?

Define each variant in its own module so names and methods stay separate, and compare them with one harness:

```julia
module V1
mysum(xs) = sum(xs)
end
module V2
function mysum(xs)
    s = zero(eltype(xs))
    for x in xs
        s += x
    end
    return s
end
end
xs = rand(1000)
V1.mysum(xs) ≈ V2.mysum(xs)
```

Warm each variant before timing. The throwaway modules keep globals and methods out of `Main`, which avoids stale-definition surprises and makes it easy to drop a variant.
What should I record next to benchmark numbers so they can be trusted later?

The things that silently change results: Julia `VERSION`, `Threads.nthreads()`, `BLAS.get_num_threads()`, the problem sizes, warm-up done or not, and the statistic (median). For example:

```julia
using LinearAlgebra
println((; julia = VERSION, threads = Threads.nthreads(), blas = BLAS.get_num_threads()))
```

If a later run disagrees, compare these values before looking at the code.
Should a quick correctness check run in a fresh process "to be safe"?

Not for routine checks. The warm session is the efficient path for correctness checks; the safety net is one cold full-suite run before the commit. A fresh process per check buys the same assurance as that single final run at many times the cost. The exceptions are Pkg operations and benchmarks that must be pinned and reproducible.
My package takes minutes to load the first time. Is that Revise?

No. A first load after the package or a dependency changed triggers precompilation, which can take minutes for heavy dependencies. Revise is not involved. Run `Pkg.precompile()` once, in the foreground with a long timeout, before creating the session. After that, `using MyPkg` loads the cached image quickly.
It is slow again after I updated a dependency.

Expected. A version change invalidates the cached images of that dependency and of everything that depends on it, so they precompile again on next load. Do the update (`Pkg.update`) and `Pkg.precompile()` in a cold foreground process, then recreate the session so it loads the new versions. Avoid doing this inside a session that has the old versions loaded.
What is the cheapest way to check that a code snippet parses?

Statically, with `julia_get_diagnostics`: it parses and lints files through the language-server analysis without compiling or running them, which costs less than any evaluation. Call `julia_set_workspace_folders` once first. For a string, `Meta.parseall(str)` in the warm session also works; syntax errors appear as `:error` or `:incomplete` nodes in the result.
My teammate says "just restart Julia whenever something is odd". When is that actually right?

When the state that is odd cannot be repaired in place:

- a compile-time preference changed (values baked into the package image),
- a struct or `const` changed on Julia 1.10 or 1.11,
- the session ran out of memory or died,
- you must change which Julia executable runs.

For everything else, repair in place: fix the source and re-evaluate, shadow a name in a fresh module, or inspect with `which`/`methods`. Restarting costs all compiled code. If you do restart, recreate with the environment `julia_list_sessions` reports.
Julia 1.12 changed something about world age. What practical effect does it have?

Global bindings now have world ages too, so redefining a struct or constant under Revise works, which removes the old "restart after every struct edit" rule on 1.12+. The flip side is a warning when running code reads a binding created after it started: "Detected access to binding ... in a world prior to its definition world", with the hint to use `Base.invokelatest`. I saw this warning in a function that `@eval`ed a definition and used it immediately on 1.13.2. Add `invokelatest` at that access, or avoid runtime `eval`.
